rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four clean, pitchable lanes without making up a single shiny detail. Its best line, "Calm built 4 million paying subscribers. Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly," turns the missing revenue terms into a real business story. B has brains, but opening with "Calm goes from $70-a-year subscription" invents a price that is nowhere in the update, and that is how you hand a reporter the knife.
gaps_in_A: The fourth angle, "Free Calm Premium reaches 25 million insurance members — if they actually use it," is useful but partly overlaps with the study-methodology angle through the "regular users" caveat.
The category angle calls it a "category-creation" story, which slightly overstates the supplied facts; the safer frame is coverage-line or benefit-design shift.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is reasonable, but the insurer names and journal citation are gating facts that should be verified before targeting real reporters.
gaps_in_B: "Calm goes from $70-a-year subscription" is an invented fact. The update says Calm Premium, not its price.
"consumer subscription apps survive once growth slows" smuggles in a growth-slowdown premise the facts do not support.
"app-store impulse buy" is cute, but it is not grounded in the update and cheapens an otherwise solid coverage-benefit angle.
The next step over-indexes on `fact-check`; useful, yes, but this set still needs angle selection and journalist-fit work after the invented-price cleanup.
